blocks.text: It is proved that בת יענה bath jaana is the female ostrich.

Next comes the bird called in Hebrew בת יענה bath jaana, as if daughter of crying, and simply יענה jaana. [col. 218] Hence the plural יענים jeenim, with a masculine ending, as יעלים jeelim, ibexes, from the feminine singular יעלה jaala. The Prophets often mention this bird among the birds that dwell in the desert. Thus it is said of Babylon in Ierem. L, 39. In it shall dwell בנות יענה, the daughters of jaana. And in Es. XIII, 21. There shall dwell the daughters of jaana. And of Idumaea, Esa. XXXIV, 13. It shall be a den of dragons, חציר לבנות יענה, a pasture of the daughters of jaana. Hence Es. XLIII, 20. The beasts of the field shall glorify me, the dragons, ובנות יענה, and the daughters of jaana. That it is a cruel bird is proved by these words of Jeremiah, Thren. IV, 3. The daughter of my people has become cruel כיענים במדבר, like the jeenim in the desert. And that it is mournful, by these words of Micah, chapter 1, verse 8: I will make a wailing like the dragons, and a mourning כבנות יענה, like the daughters of jaana. With this very passage in view, Job says in chapter 30, verse 29: I was a brother of dragons, and a companion לבנות יענה, of the daughters of jaana. This is what the sacred writers say of bath jaana and jeenim.

The Greek translators render it sirens in Micah, in Jeremiah, and in Esa. XIII, 21. On this passage Cyril says: Σειρῆνας δὲ, οἶμαι, φησὶ τὰ εὔστομεῖν εἰδότα πτηνὰ, ἢ κατά γε τὴν Ἑβραίων ἔκδοσιν, τὴν γλαῦκα· [Seirēnas de, oimai, phēsi ta eustomein eidota ptēna, ē kata ge tēn Hebraiōn ekdosin, tēn glauka] By sirens he means, I think, birds skilled in singing, or, according to the Hebrew edition, the little owl. And the same author on Mich. I, 8., after discussing the sirens of the poets, says: Ἡ δέ γε θεόπνευστος γραφὴ Σειρῆνας καλεῖ τὰ τῶν στρουθίων λαλίστατά τε, καὶ εὐστομεῖν εἰωθότα, ἢ καὶ αὐτὰς ἔσθ᾽ ὅτε τὰς ἀηδόνας, αἱ τοῖς ἐναλίοις ἐπωάζουσαι κόλποις. εἶτα τῆς καλιᾶς λεφθείσης ὑπὸ κυμάτων, γοερὸν ᾄδουσι μέλος, καὶ καταθρήνουσι τρόπον τινα τὴν τῆς ἑαυτῶν ὠδῖνος ζημίαν. [Hē de ge theopneustos graphē Seirēnas kalei ta tōn strouthiōn lalistata te, kai eustomein eiōthota, ē kai autas esth᾽ hote tas aēdonas, hai tois enaliois epōazousai kolpois. eita tēs kalias lephtheisēs hypo kymatōn, goeron adousi melos, kai katathrēnousi tropon tina tēn tēs heautōn ōdinos zēmian.] But the sacred Scripture calls sirens the most eloquent and most tuneful of small birds, or at times the nightingales themselves, which brood their eggs at the edges of the sea. Then, when the nest has been swept away by the waves, they pour forth a mournful song, and in a way lament the loss of their brood. In these words you will wonder why he writes that τὰς ἀηδόνας [tas aēdonas], nightingales, which have nothing in common with the sea and the waves, brood their eggs at the edges of the sea and lament for their nest swept away by the waves. Since this is plainly out of place, at my own risk read τὰς ἀλκυόνας [tas alkyonas] instead of τὰς ἀηδόνας [tas aēdonas]. For he is following Chrysostom, who, on these words of Job, chapter 30, verse 29, Ἀδελφὸς γέγονα Σειρήνων [Adelphos gegona Seirēnōn], explains the word sirens thus: Σειρῆνας λέγει ᾠδικάς τινας ὄρνιθας, ἀλκυόνας, ἢ γλαῦκας· ἄμφω γὰρ θρηνητικά. [Seirēnas legei ōdikas tinas ornithas, alkyonas, ē glaukas; amphō gar thrēnētika.] By sirens he means certain tuneful birds, namely halcyons, [II, 812] or little owls; for both are mournful. And I do not know by what fate it has come about that, although ἀλκυὼν [alkyōn] and ἀηδὼν [aēdōn] are words quite different in spelling, they are nevertheless not rarely confused by copyists. Thus in Aristotle, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 2, where the more recent editions rightly read Τὸ τῶν ἀλκυόνων δὲ γένος πάρυδρόν ἐστι· [To tōn alkyonōn de genos parydron esti] The kind of halcyons lives near the waters: the older editions wrongly read τῶν ἀηδόνων [tōn aēdonōn] instead of τῶν ἀλκυόνων [tōn alkyonōn]. And when in Suidas, under Ἡμερινὰ ζῶα [Hēmerina zōa], ἀλκυὼν, ἀηδὼν, κήυκες [alkyōn, aēdōn, kēykes], halcyon, nightingale, ceyces, are listed among sea birds, the word ἀηδὼν [aēdōn] is nothing but a variant reading of the word ἀλκυὼν [alkyōn], first noted in the margin and then intruded into the text. With these observations made, Cyril's words will be plain and clear: since the sirens in the poets have in part the shape of birds, [col. 219] a station on the seashore, and a wonderful sweetness of song, he holds that the interpreters of Scripture mean by the name sirens the halcyons, shore birds that are very tuneful. Accordingly, Chaeremon in Lucian's Halcyon says of its voice: Ὡς ἡδεῖα ταῖς ἀκοαῖς! [Hōs hēdeia tais akoais!] How pleasant it is to hear! And in the Images the same Lucian says that a certain woman sings so sweetly to the cithara that, when she sings something, it is ὥρα σιωπᾶν ταῦτα ἀλκυόσι, καὶ τέττιξι, καὶ τοῖς κύκνοις [hōra siōpan tauta alkyosi, kai tettixi, kai tois kyknois], time for the halcyons, the cicadas and the swans to be silent. Plutarch likewise, in the book Utra anim.: Ποίας γὰρ ἀηδόνας (παραβάλλειν) ἄξιον τῷ φιλομούσῳ τῆς ἀλκυόνος; [Poias gar aēdonas (paraballein) axion tō philomousō tēs alkyonos?] For what nightingales could be compared with the halcyon in respect of song? And Oppian asserts that no bird sings more sweetly. So in the Anthology, book 3, chapter 24, Tymnaeus, to praise a bird as highly as possible for the charm of its song, says that it equals the song of the halcyons:
Ὄρνεον ὦ χάρισιν μεμελημένον, ὦ παρόμοιον Ἀλκυόσιν τὸν σὸν φθόγγον ἰσωσάμενον. [Orneon ō charisin memelēmenon, ō paromoion Alkyosin ton son phthongon isōsamenon.]
Cyril adds that halcyons brood their eggs at the edges of the sea and, when the nest is swept away by the waves, pour forth a mournful song; as Valerius Flaccus in book 4 of the Argonautica:
